abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: As a major cause of cancer-related morbidity in women, cervical cancer is strongly related to chronic infection by high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). This viral persistence also underpins the pathogenesis of a broad spectrum of cancers. In this review, we summarize the research progress of prophylactic and therapeutic HPV vaccines in clinical trials. Furthermore, we present a critical analysis of future challenges, specifically discussing the type replacement phenomenon and its potential implications for long-term vaccine efficacy. We also expand the discourse to a pan-gender and pan-cancer scope, rigorously evaluating the necessity of gender-inclusive vaccination in the context of rising HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers. To overcome real-world implementation barriers, next-generation design strategies, such as chimeric virus-like particles, HPV L2-based vaccines, and heterologous prime-boost immunotherapy regimens for therapeutic HPV vaccines, should be expedited into clinical trials. In summary, this review provides a comprehensive perspective and a forward-looking roadmap for the immunotherapy of HPV-related malignancies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cervical cancer (CC) is the fourth leading cancer that primarily impairs younger women’s reproductive and sexual health worldwide, with its highest incidence occurring between ages 35 and 44, and a median diagnosis age of 50 y.1 In 2022, an estimated 660,000 new cases and 350,000 related CC deaths were reported globally.2 The incidence and mortality rates of CC are significantly correlated with the socioeconomic status,3 for example, there is a 3.4-fold difference in the age-standardized incidence of CC between high-income countries (HICs) (3.1) and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) (10.6).2 This phenomenon stems from multiple contributing factors, including disparities in access to national human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programs, CC screening and treatment services, as well as socioeconomic determinants.4

Decades of researches have confirmed that persistent infection with certain types of HPV is a necessary cause of CC.5 In addition to being a necessary cause of CC, HPV infection also accounts for a substantial fraction of other malignancies, such as anal, head and neck (HAN), vaginal, vulvar, and penile cancers.6 These cancers associated public health burden has driven extensive prevention and therapeutic research. Notably, CC is the first malignancy recognized as susceptible to elimination through widespread vaccination with prophylactic and therapeutic HPV vaccines. Strategies employed in the prevention of this cancer offer a valuable framework for the management of other cancer types.

Unlike prophylactic vaccines which stimulate the production of L1/L2-specific neutralizing antibodies to prevent HPV infection, therapeutic vaccines aim to elicit a cellular immune response against existing HPV infections and associated lesions.7 The early protein E6 and E7 are essential for maintaining the oncogenic potential of HPV. They are consistently expressed in infected and cancerous cells but are absent or expressed only at minimal levels in normal cells, making them ideal tumor-specific antigens.8 To eliminate CC as a public health challenge by 2030, World Health Organization (WHO) launched a global framework that is referred to as the 90–70–90 targets.6 This framework sets specific goals: ensuring 90% of girls are vaccinated against HPV by age 15; screening 70% of women with high-quality tests at ages 35 and 45; and achieving 90% treatment coverage for women with CC. Since then, a large number of clinical trials have been conducted to investigate the effectiveness of HPV vaccines in preventing and treating infections and related cancers. However, the challenges associated with implementing immunization programs in the post-vaccination era are not summarized.

In this review, we systematically summarize the latest progress of prophylactic and therapeutic HPV vaccines in clinical trials, with a focus on elaborating the advantages and disadvantages of various vaccines as well as vaccine efficacy endpoints. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the existing challenges in the real-world implementation of prophylactic HPV vaccines. The global disparity in access to these vaccines, coupled with their limited cross-protection, has accelerated the development of next-generation candidates, such as chimeric virus-like particles (chVLPs) and L2-based vaccines. Moreover, future studies must carefully investigate the impact of type replacement phenomenon and its consequences for vaccine effectiveness in the post-vaccination era. Given the increasing incidence of other HPV-related cancers, particularly oropharyngeal cancer in men, we underscore the critical need for pan-gender vaccination programs and assess the prevent effect of HPV vaccination on all HPV-related cancers. Moving forward, our discussion prioritizes heterologous prime-boost immunotherapy strategies for therapeutic HPV vaccines, aiming to lay the groundwork for the targeted elimination of HPV-associated cancers.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This review conducted a systematic literature search across PubMed, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov. The search strategy employed a comprehensive combination of keywords, including ‘Human Papillomavirus,’ ‘Cervical Cancer,’ and specific vaccine nomenclature (e.g., ‘Prophylactic HPV Vaccine,’ ‘Bivalent/Quadrivalent/Nonavalent HPV Vaccine’). Additionally, terms related to therapeutic modalities such as ‘Therapeutic HPV Vaccine,’ ‘Vector Vaccines,’ ‘Peptide/Protein Vaccines,’ and ‘Nucleic Acid-based Vaccines (DNA/mRNA)’ were incorporated.

The search was specifically tailored to identify studies evaluating the real-world effectiveness of prophylactic vaccines and clinical research on therapeutic vaccines. For therapeutic interventions, the focus was on clinical outcomes including objective response rates, histological regression of lesions, and overall survival (OS).

The analysis of existing challenges was based on: (1) the systematic extraction of limitations, unmet needs, and technical bottlenecks explicitly reported in the included studies; (2) the thematic categorization of these challenges into key domains, such as limited cross-protection, high production costs, national immunization programs, and real-world vaccination coverage gaps; (3) the critical synthesis of consensus and discrepancies across studies, such as the type replacement phenomenon, supported by recent clinical trial data and authoritative reviews; (4) the identification of research gaps, specifically where the observed decline in CC incidence among women, contrasted with the rising trends in HAN and penile cancers in men, highlighting the critical role of pan-gender vaccination programs in controlling HPV-related cancers.

sec.title: Prophylactic HPV vaccines
sec.p:
Currently, seven HPV vaccines are available to prevent infections that may lead to cancer: Cervarix, Cecolin, Walrinvax (bivalent), Gardasil, Cervavac (quadrivalent) and Gardasil-9, Cecolin-9 (nonavalent) vaccine (Table 1). All the prophylactic HPV vaccines are based on virus-like particles (VLPs). By self-assembling L1 capsid proteins that form a regular icosahedron, VLPs may closely mimic native HPV particles and induce a 10-fold higher antibody titer compared with natural infection, thereby contributing to protection.9Table 1.

sec.title: Efficacy and effectiveness of HPV vaccinations from clinical trials
Bivalent vaccine
sec.p: A large, international phase III study demonstrated that the vaccine efficacy of the bivalent vaccine was 90.4% against cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 2 (CIN 2) caused by HPV16/18 (NCT00122681).10 Moreover, the bivalent vaccine showed cross-protection against non-covered HPV types such as HPV31/33/45.11 In addition to invasive CC, the bivalent HPV vaccine also showed excellent vaccine efficacy (76.9%) against all cases of adenocarcinoma in situ or the total vaccinated cohort.12 Two long-term follow-up studies assessed the protective effectiveness of bivalent vaccine against CIN 2 and CIN 3 caused by covered and non-covered HPV types (NCT00867464).13 Interestingly, compared with the unvaccinated group, the rates of cervical precancer caused by non-covered HPV types in the vaccinated group increased by 8.3 per 1,000 vaccinated participants (NCT00128661, NCT00867464).14 Another rare cancer, anal cancer, caused by HPV types 16 or 18, but its incidence rates are rising in many countries. No difference was found in the efficacy of the bivalent HPV vaccine against anal infection compared to that against cervical infection (NCT00128661).15

sec.title: Quadrivalent vaccine
sec.p: The quadrivalent vaccine markedly lessened the risk of high-grade vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) and vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia associated with HPV16/18 in a heterogeneous group of women with and without HPV exposure (NCT00365716, NCT00092521, NCT00092534).16–18 For boys and men from 16 to 26 y of age, the efficacy of the quadrivalent vaccine in preventing the infection of external genital lesions and anogenital HPV was 65.5%, whether or not the subjects had been infected with HPV. However, in the subjects who were negative for involved HPV types at enrollment, the efficacy was 90.4% (NCT00090285).19 A long-term follow-up study has indicated that the quadrivalent vaccine is not only appropriate for young adolescents, but also beneficial for unvaccinated adult men who have been previously exposed to HPV (catch-up vaccination populations). Reported cases per 10,000 person-years of external genital warts in the catch-up vaccination populations decreased from 155.1 to 0 (NCT00090285).20,21

sec.title: Nonavalent vaccine
sec.p: Compared with the quadrivalent vaccine, the antibody responses induced by the nonavalent HPV vaccine were noninferior against HPV types 6/11/16/18. However, the nonavalent HPV vaccine did not prevent infection and disease caused by the non-vaccine HPV types (NCT00543543).22 There were no significant differences in antibody responses among Chinese females aged 9–19, 20–26, or 27–45 y.23 But immunogenicity analyses of males (NCT00543543, NCT01651949, NCT01984697, NCT02114385) revealed higher geometric mean titers of antibodies against nine HPV types in heterosexual men compared with men who have sex with men.24 A 10-y post-vaccination follow-up study (NCT00943722) further demonstrated that the nonavalent HPV vaccine induces sustained antibody responses and durable protective efficacy.25 In LMICs, the accessibility of nonavalent HPV vaccine faces numerous challenges as a result of the high cost and low production supply of Gardasil-9. Cecolin-9, a robust and cost-effective nonavalent HPV vaccine, produced in the Escherichia coli expression system, was used to prevent HPV infections. A head-to-head study between Cecolin-9 and Gardasil-9 found that there was no difference in terms of HPV type-specific immune responses (NCT04782895).26

sec.title: What is the vaccination strategy for prophylactic HPV vaccine? Single-dose, two-doses or three-doses?
sec.p: Single-dose vaccination strategy could decrease vaccination costs, increase vaccine coverage, and simplify the vaccination schedule. Moreover, the administration of two-doses or even three-doses of HPV vaccine is a challenge in LMICs due to the high cost and low production supply of the vaccine. Two randomized clinical trials were conducted to evaluate the protective effect of one-dose, two-doses and three-doses post-immunization in young women aged 15–25 y (NCT00128661, NCT00122681).27 For the vaccine HPV type 16/18 infections, the protection effect of one-dose or two-doses of bivalent or quadrivalent vaccine was similar to the three-dose schedule (NCT00923702).28–30 However, for infections with non-vaccine HPV types such as HPV-31/33/45, the protective effect of three-dose schedule (59.7%) was higher than the one-dose (37.7%) or two-dose groups (36.6%). A single-dose HPV vaccination program for girls and boys aged 9 to 20 y was endorsed by the WHO.31

sec.title: Real-world effectiveness and herd protection studies
sec.p: A nationwide registry of real-world data from Sweden and Denmark found that the quadrivalent vaccine significantly reduced the risk of invasive CC for girls and women aged 15–34.32,33 Furthermore, compared with women aged 20–30 who received the vaccine, girls under the age of 20 showed a higher preventive effect against CC, which highlights the importance of early vaccination.33 Since a national HPV vaccination program was implemented in Australia in 2007, the proportion of new genital warts diagnoses had reduced by 64% by 2018 relative to the pre-vaccination era in sexual health clinics.34 The most astonishing fact is that the proportions of new genital warts diagnoses in women and men under the age of 21 in patients born in Australia decreased by 98% and 92% respectively, which is attributed to the high vaccination coverage rate in Australia (80% for females and 76% for males).35 And a mere 21% reduction was noted among overseas-born patients from countries without an HPV vaccination program, emphasizing the crucial role of herd protection.36,37 However, a substantial disparity existed in the proportion of countries that had implemented national HPV vaccination programs between HICs and LMICs by 2019 (88% versus 30%),38 largely due to the significant reluctance of LMICs to the national immunization programs. This resistance was triggered by inadequate planning, weak communication strategies, and widespread public skepticism. As of 2023, HPV vaccination coverage among girls in LMICs stood at only 20%,39 posing a major barrier to achieving herd-level protection against HPV-related diseases.

sec.title: Future challenges of prophylactic HPV vaccines
sec.p: While progress in prophylactic HPV vaccine development and initial implementation has been notable, a key challenge warranting explicit attention is the unequal global distribution of prophylactic HPV vaccines, particularly the nonavalent vaccine (Gardasil-9). This limited access stems from multiple barriers: high costs, fragmented supply chains, and insufficient prioritization in national immunization programs.39 Currently, dual approaches are being pursued to bridge this gap between HICs and LMICs: technological innovations and optimized vaccination strategies. On the technological front, efforts include: (1) developing capsomere-hybrid virus-like particles (chVLPs) capable of conferring multi-type HPV protection via a single construct40,41; (2) using prokaryotic expression systems to lower production costs.26 In parallel, public health strategies such as adopting a single-dose vaccination regimen are being implemented to improve coverage in LMICs.42 Notably, using neutralizing epitope transplantation and epitope resurfacing technologies, the nine-valent chVLPs vaccine has been shown to elicit neutralizing antibody titers comparable to those induced by Gardasil-9.43 Furthermore, the L2 protein offers distinct advantages: it is highly conserved across a broad range of HPV types and, due to its structural simplicity, can be produced at a lower cost than the L1 protein.44 Although naturally less immunogenic, the L2 protein can elicit robust immune responses when formulated with appropriate adjuvants. Consequently, L2-based HPV vaccines hold promise for overcoming the narrow spectrum of protection offered by current prophylactic vaccines.45

There has been some debate about whether HPV types not covered by the vaccine (so-called type replacement) have risen in vaccinated populations. Two randomized trials analyzed the incidence of non-covered HPV infections after implementation of the bivalent vaccine, finding that incidence rates caused by non-covered oncogenic types were lower than in the control group (NCT00128661, NCT00122681).46 This research indicated that type replacement is improbable among individuals who have received the vaccine. Two other recent long-term studies have also corroborated this finding.47,48 Nonetheless, another study reported that CC cases induced by non-covered oncogenic HPV types increased notably compared with the pre-vaccination periods in Stockholm.49 A 10-long follow-up investigation assess the impact of bivalent HPV vaccine immunization on the high risk-HPV infection profiles and natural history, revealing a notable elevation in non-covered type HPV 52 associated lesions in the vaccine group compared with the control group.50 Moreover, an increase in non-covered oncogenic types is more likely to be observed in populations with high sexual activity, emphasizing the necessity of early monitoring.51 When evaluating the appearance of HPV type replacement between the post-vaccination and pre-vaccination era, many factors need to be taken into consideration, such as the population selection bias, vaccine-induced cross-protection and the indirect impacts of herd protection.48

Due to early detection and treatment of precancerous conditions during screening and follow-up, the rate of CC in the United States has been descending, especially in younger women. In contrast, the rate of oropharyngeal and anal/rectal cancer has increased among older men.52 Oropharyngeal cancer has become the most prevalent cancer linked to HPV, with most cases attributed to HPV16.53 Additionally, a significant proportion of other HPV 16/18-associated cancers, specifically HAN cancers, are also exhibiting increasing incidence in the male population.54,55 These trends underscore the critical importance of pan-gender vaccination programs. Consequently, a growing number of countries have included adolescent boys in their national immunization schedules, a strategy predicted to enhance overall coverage and accelerate the elimination of HPV-associated cancers.56 Despite these advances, research on the effectiveness of HPV vaccination against non-cervical cancers remains limited, partly because these malignancies are typically diagnosed at later ages.57 Moreover, the protective potential of prophylactic HPV vaccination against certain malignancies, such as penile cancer, remains undetermined,58 largely due to the rarity of these cases and historically low vaccination coverage among males (approximately 4% as of 2019).59 Nevertheless, emerging evidence suggests efficacy: the quadrivalent HPV vaccine has demonstrated superior protection against HPV-associated oral infections compared to unvaccinated controls, with a two- or three-dose regimen proving more effective than a single dose.60,61 In 2020, the U.S. FDA approved the nonavalent HPV vaccine for the prevention of HPV-related oropharyngeal and HAN cancers. Currently, two ongoing clinical trials have been designed and are being conducted in immunocompetent men (NCT04199689)62 and in men infected with human immunodeficiency virus (NCT04255849).63

sec.title: Vector-based vaccines
sec.p: Vector-based vaccines can be classified into two categories: viral vector and bacterial vector. These attenuated live vector systems can replicate in host cells and express the target genes, thereby inducing a strong humoral and cellular immune response.64 However, there are two problems to consider in clinical application: possible safety concerns for immunocompromised individuals and preexisting antibodies to the vector itself.65

TG4001, a modified vaccinia virus (MVA) vector, which encodes the early genes E6 and E7 of HPV 16 as well as the human interleukin-2 gene, can effectively eliminate CIN 2/3 cytological lesions and clear HPV 16 mRNA (NCT01022346).66,67 Regardless of initial HPV infection status, the vaccine group showed higher viral DNA clearance than the placebo group. Furthermore, TG4001 can be used in combination with avelumab (anti-programmed cell death protein ligand-1 antibody) to treat patients with incurable anogenital cancer.68 The randomized phase II trial is currently being evaluated (NCT03260023). A live recombinant vaccinia virus expressing HPV16/18 E6 and E7 proteins, TA-HPV, can induce HPV specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses in the CC patients (NCT00002916).69 Other virus-based vectors, such as Semliki Forest virus (NCT03141463), lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (NCT04180215), gorilla adenovirus (NCT04432597), Chimpanzee Adenovirus (NCT04607850), Oncolytic MG1 Virus (NCT03618953), and adenovirus serotype 26 (NCT03610581), have already entered phase I trials.

ADXS11-001, a genetically modified live-attenuated Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) that secretes HPV-16 E7 antigen linked to a non-lytic fragment of the Lm’s listeriolysin, was approved to treat invasive carcinoma of the cervix in 2009.70 The treatment group exhibited improved survival curves compared to historical data, with the median OS increasing from 4.7 to 8.3 months.71 In addition, ADXS11-001 also treats other HPV-caused cancers, such as oropharyngeal cancer (NCT02002182), anal cancer (NCT02399813), and persistent or recurrent CC (NCT01266460). Unlike the intramuscular ADXS11-001 vaccine, some oral vaccines based on Lactococcus lactis or Lactobacillus casei, such as GLBL101c and IGMKK16E7 can also be used for the treatment of CIN 2/3.72,73 These vaccines were able to elicit E7-specific mucosal immunity in the uterine cervical lesions, leading to a pathological reduction to CIN 2 in 70% of patients who received the optimized doses.74

sec.title: Peptide-based vaccines
sec.p: There are several benefits of peptide-based vaccines, particularly in terms of their stability, safety, and the simplicity of their production and storage. In order to elicit a stronger immune response, peptide-based vaccines are typically combined with immunomodulatory adjuvants.75

Conjugated to the toll-like receptor 2 ligand adjuvant (Amplivant), HPV16-synthetic long peptide vaccine, comprising both T helper (Th) and cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) epitopes, induced antigen-specific T cell responses in a dose-dependent manner (NCT02821494).76 Another long peptide vaccine, ISA101, showed tumor regression in 43% of 72 evaluable patients with recurrent CC receiving combined chemotherapy.77 The intensity of type 1 T cell responses is positively correlated with the prolonged survival of patients. Currently, ISA101 vaccine in combination with cemiplimab (an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody) is being evaluated for its treatment effect for HPV16-positive cancers, such as oropharyngeal cancer (NCT04398524, NCT03669718), and CC (NCT04646005). Relative to the placebo group, patients treated with the combination therapy who had a pre-treatment programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) combined positive score ≥20 exhibited superior outcomes: an objective response rate (ORR) of 51.7% versus 25.8%, and a prolonged median OS of 34.8 months versus 28.8 months.78 These results suggest that this combination regimen may be particularly beneficial for patients with higher tumor cell PD-L1 expression.79 PepCan consists of four synthetic HPV 16 E6 protein peptides and an adjuvant derived from the colorless extract of Candida albicans (Candin®). The vaccine induced the production of T-helper type 1 cells and the histological regression rate was 45% overall. Of note, in the cohort of 12 patients with baseline HPV16 positivity, treatment led to a significant decrease in viral load in nine individuals and complete clearance in three.80 Now, two phase II studies are being conducted to assess the therapeutic effect of PepCan against cervical high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) (NCT02481414) and HAN cancer (NCT03821272). In addition to the long peptide vaccine, some short peptide vaccines are also undergoing clinical trials, such as liposomal-based vaccine (PDS0101), and DepoVax adjuvant-based vaccine (DPX-E7).

sec.title: Protein-based vaccines
sec.p: Compared to peptide vaccines, protein-based vaccines overcome MHC restriction by harboring abundant CD4+ and CD8+ T cell epitopes. Nevertheless, their major drawback is a bias toward inducing humoral antibody responses over cellular CTL responses. Tissue antigen-cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (TA-CIN), a fusion protein subunit vaccine containing HPV 16 L2, E6, and E7 proteins, was combined with TA-HPV for the immunotherapy of HPV 16-associated VIN.81 A bivalent therapeutic vaccine, GTL001 (also called ProCervix), is formulated with HPV16 and HPV18 E7 proteins displayed on the Bordetella pertussis adenylate cyclase (CyaA) vector (NCT01957878). Now the study was terminated due to the lack of significant difference in terms of viral clearance rates between the treatment and placebo groups (NCT02689726). SGN-00101, alternatively named HSP-E7, is constructed by fusing HPV16 E7 with recombinant heat shock protein 65 derived from Mycobacterium bovis. This vaccine demonstrated clinical activity in anal intraepithelial neoplasia (NCT00052897),82 CIN 3 (NCT00075569, NCT00054041),83 and cervical HSIL,84 manifesting as elevated HPV-specific CTL counts and regression of high-grade lesions.

sec.title: Cell-based vaccines
sec.p: Cell-based vaccines can adoptively transfer autologous antigen-specific cells (APCs) that express target antigens to the patient, thereby generating antigen-specific cellular responses.75 However, the development of cell-based vaccines also faces many challenges, such as HLA compatibility issues, the time-consuming process of developing personalized cell-based therapies, and the high costs associated with scaling treatment to large patient populations.64

A phase I study was conducted on patients with recurrent or persistent CC, who were alternately immunized with HPV E7 lipopeptide epitope vaccine and dendritic cells (DCs) vaccine presenting E7 epitopes (NCT00003977). Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were also used for the treatment of HPV-caused cancers, such as cancers of the cervix, vagina, penis, anus, esophagus, or HAN (NCT00019110). SQZ-PBMC-HPV, an autologous cell vaccine, was engineered by SQZ Biotechnologies via microfluidic squeezing technology, which enables loading of HPV16 E6 and E7 antigens into PBMCs for HLA-A*02+ patients.85 Among the eighteen patients who received single-agent treatment with SQZ-PBMC-HPV, six cases (33%) showed an increase in CD8+ T cell density in tumor parenchyma, which may contribute to a higher disease control rate (DCR) (66.7% vs 16.7%) and a longer OS (606.5 d vs 170.0 d). Moreover, SQZ-PBMC-HPV was used in combination with some immune checkpoint inhibitors to treat locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors (NCT04084951). The BVAC-C immunotherapeutic vaccine, which uses B cells and monocytes as APCs to load recombinant HPV E6/E7, was then transfused back into patients to treat recurrent or metastatic CC (NCT02866006). Upon vaccination, all studied patients displayed not only inflammatory cytokine release (IFN-γ or TNF-α) but also potent E6/E7-specific T cell responses. Furthermore, the DCR and median OS of the BVAC-C immunotherapeutic vaccine were 53.8% and 17.7 months respectively.86

In recent years, a variety of T cell therapy strategies including adoptive transfer of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells and T cell receptor (TCR)-T cells were employed to treat of HPV-associated cancers.87,88 In nine patients who were treated with a single infusion of tumor-infiltrating T cells expressing HPV E6 and E7 proteins, two patients completely degraded the cancer, and these responses persisted for over 22 and 15 months, respectively (NCT01585428).89,90 Additionally, the TIL therapy targeting CC has received breakthrough therapy designation from the FDA.87 An I/II phase study on engineered T cells expressing T cell receptors (TCRs) targeting the HPV16 E6 protein for the treatment of HPV-related metastatic epithelial cancer showed that only two out of twelve patients (16.7%) achieved significant tumor regression (NCT02280811). However, TCR-engineered T cells targeting the E7 oncoprotein significantly improved the proportion of patients with epithelial cancers experiencing tumor regression (from 16.7% to 50%) (NCT02858310).91 A multi-center clinical trial on the treatment of CC with modified CAR-T cells was conducted in patients with GD2, PSMA, Muc1, Mesothelin or other markers (NCT03356795).

sec.title: DNA-based vaccines
sec.p: By employing a shuttle system containing optimized gene sequences encoding HPV E6 or E7 and a eukaryotic promoter, DNA vaccines can be administered via intradermal or intramuscular injection to directly express antigen proteins in target cells. They exhibit several advantages, such as their safety and tolerance for all patient groups, ease of production and the ability to add multiple plasmids encoding diverse antigens.92 However, these vaccines have low transfection efficiency; specialized vaccination equipment is required, and additional adjuvants are required to strengthen the immune response.8

A first therapeutic DNA vaccine, VGX-3100, delivers HPV-16/18 E6/E7 proteins into myocytes to elicit an effector T cell response using electroporation technology, which led to histopathological regression for women with CIN 2/3 in a phase 2b trial (NCT01304524).93,94 Most (32/35; 91%) participants who were treated with VGX-3100 exhibited cervical high-grade HSIL regression and an undetectable HPV-16/18 at 18 months, thereby avoiding excision surgery at the end of study (NCT01304524).95 GX-188E, a DNA vaccine encoding a tissue plasminogen activator signal sequence, Fms-like tyrosine kinase-3 ligand and HPV-16/18 E6/E7 antigens, was used to treat HPV-16/18-associated malignancies. More than half of the patients showed histologic regression and HPV clearance after treatment, which was positively associated with the levels of IFN-γ ELISpot responses (NCT02139267).96 The GX-188E DNA vaccine combined with pembrolizumab (NCT03444376) or nivolumab (NCT05280457) was used to evaluate the anti-tumor activity in patients with recurrent or advanced CC.97 This combination therapy exhibited a favorable OS (23.8 months) and ORR (35.0%).98 VB10.16 is a modular DNA vaccine that encodes a recombinant protein composed of HPV16 E6/E7 proteins and the natural human chemokine ligand 3-like 1. In 17 evaluable subjects, it induced a strong IFN-γ T-cell response in 16 cases (94%), thereby significantly reducing the size of the lesion (NCT02529930).99 The VB10.16 therapeutic DNA vaccine combined with an immune checkpoint inhibitor atezolizumab was effective for the patients with persistent, recurrent or metastatic HPV16-positive CC, especially if PD-L1-positive (NCT04405349).100 Composed of two plasmids encoding both HPV-6/11 E6/E7 and interleukin-12 genes, respectively, INO-3107, a DNA immunotherapy vaccine, can elicit durable CD4 and CD8 T cell responses after intramuscular injection followed by electroporation delivery.101 Recent studies demonstrated that INO-3107 can significantly decrease the number of surgical interventions for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) associated with HPV6/11 after treatment (NCT04398433).102,103

sec.title: mRNA-based vaccines
sec.p: To date, most of mRNA-based therapeutic HPV vaccines are in the clinical trial stage, though several phase I/II trials have generated promising findings for historically poorly immunogenic tumors.104 Because tumor-associated antigens are directly delivered into the cytoplasm and translated into target proteins, mRNA-based HPV vaccines can induce a strong immune response.105 Therefore, mRNA-based vaccines show promise for developing personalized therapeutic vaccines due to the rapid design and production capabilities, high versatility in modifying sequences to target specific antigens, and rapidly matched to the unique tumor profiles of individual patients.106 During the COVID-19 pandemic, mRNA vaccines developed by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna exhibited remarkable clinical efficacy in preventing COVID-19, a success largely attributable to their capacity to rapidly elicit potent immune responses.107 However, promptly identifying neoantigens, effectively delivering them into cells, regulating the balance between immunogenicity and safety, and overcoming tumor heterogeneity and the dynamic tumor microenvironment remain challenges for mRNA-based therapeutic vaccines.105

BNT113, a liposomal RNA vaccine encoding HPV-16 E6/E7 oncoproteins, is currently being combined with pembrolizumab or anti-CD40 antibodies to evaluate the safety, tolerability and therapeutic efficacy of HPV-16 positive cancer (NCT04534205, NCT03418480). Another mRNA-based therapeutic vaccine, RG002, is now being used to evaluate the efficacy in treating HPV16/18-related CIN 2/3 (NCT06273553).

sec.title: Future perspectives of therapeutic HPV vaccines
sec.p: It is difficult to make parallel comparisons of therapeutic effects for various vaccines because in clinical trials, the immunization methods, doses and means of evaluating the therapeutic effects for each vaccine are very different. It must be acknowledged that each type of therapeutic HPV vaccine has its own advantages and disadvantages. In order to fully utilize the advantages of various vaccines and generate a more robust immune response, the combined use of multiple vaccine platforms (heterologous prime-boost immunotherapy strategy) is worthy of further research and development.75

Preclinical study of heterologous prime-boost vaccination project in mice demonstrated that this combination strategy strongly increased antigen specific T cell responses, such as peptide with viral vector vaccine, mRNA with oncolytic virus vector vaccine, and DNA with protein vaccine.108–110 However, the increased number of antigen specific CTL cannot contribute to improve the antitumor responses.111 For the clinical study, a heterologous HPV vaccination regimen in which women were vaccinated with a protein vaccine (TA-CIN) followed by a vaccinia virus vector vaccine (TA-HPV) was used in the management of anogenital intraepithelial neoplasia.112 There was no difference in immune response between heterologous vaccination group and single TA-HPV vaccination group. In another similar study, these vaccines were used in the opposite sequence for the treatment of VIN. Although patients showed an increase in HPV-specific T cells after the TA-CIN booster vaccination, these responses were not correlated with the clinical regression of VIN.81 A phase II trial was conducted to investigate the treatment of HPV16-positive low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL)/CIN 1, involving participants initially primed with the pNGVL4a-Sig/E7(detox)/HSP70 DNA vaccine followed by a boost with the recombinant protein vaccine TA-CIN.113 Surprisingly, this combination vaccine enhanced HPV16 viral clearance rates, exceeding expectations at both 6- and 12-months post-treatment. However, this conclusion warrants further validation, as the trial was limited by the absence of a control or placebo group and a small sample size. Moreover, the paucity of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating HPV vaccine efficacy has resulted in insufficient evidence to support their therapeutic potential for advanced CC. To mitigate this methodological imbalance and evidence gap, targeted interventions are urgently needed. For example, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration between clinicians and vaccine researchers is critical, coupled with the development of standardized experimental protocols that adhere strictly to ethical and scientific principles. In addition, another three heterologous HPV vaccination regimen, pNGVL4a-Sig/E7(Detox)/HSP70 DNA and TA-HPV (NCT06508138), pBI-11 DNA and TA-HPV (NCT05799144), pNGVL4aCRTE6E7L2 DNA and TA-CIN (NCT03913117) are currently recruiting volunteers.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this review, we provide an overview of challenges encountered following the of the prophylactic and therapeutic HPV vaccines in the real-world, with a particular focus on cofactors driving type replacement in the post-vaccination era. There is still a long way to go to achieve the goal of global eradication of HPV-associated cancers.114,115 Although prophylactic HPV vaccines have achieved significant success in preventing infections, several critical issues remain to be addressed, such as the limited protection spectrum and the financial barriers to vaccine access in LMICs. To advance global immunization agendas, sustained investment is urgently needed to accelerate the development of next-generation vaccines, such as chVLPs and L2-based candidates that offer broader cross-protection, enhanced immunogenicity, and improved affordability. And future clinical trials should emphasize pan-gender vaccination programs and the preventive efficacy of HPV vaccines against all HPV-related cancers. In contrast, therapeutic HPV vaccine development has progressed at a slower pace, with few candidates achieving clinical validation. Future trials must prioritize three key areas: (1) mechanistic studies linking antigen-specific immune responses to clinically meaningful endpoints (e.g., histological regression, OS); (2) optimization of heterologous prime-boost strategies to amplify B and T-cell immunity; and (3) advancement of mRNA-based platforms capable of balancing personalized neoantigen targeting with scalable manufacturing.104 Addressing these challenges will be essential to bridge the gap between prophylactic success and therapeutic innovation in the fight against HPV-associated cancers.
